items.title: L7: Sequencing the steps from offer to first day
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Between a conditional offer and your first day, several things happen in a fairly predictable order, and mistakes usually come from getting the order wrong. First you accept the offer in the way the letter says. Next the checks team asks for your BPSS information and documents, and, if the role needs it, sponsors you for clearance so that the vetting service can send you a questionnaire. Referees and past employers are contacted in parallel. Only when the department has what it needs does it issue an unconditional offer or confirm that you can start, sometimes with restrictions while clearance is pending.

Two habits matter. First, hold off on irreversible personal decisions, such as giving notice, until the department confirms in writing that you can start. Second, respond to every request with the complete answer and the right documents, because a partial reply restarts the clock. If a request is unclear, ask a question rather than guess.

Your own notice period sets the earliest realistic date. If your current contract needs a month's notice and the department cannot confirm a start date, the sensible course is to ask what is likely and when, not to resign and hope. Some departments will agree a later start date if your notice is long. Others have a fixed intake. Either way, the offer letter and the checks team, not the advert, are the authority on dates.

Finally, keep the checks team informed of anything that changes, since a surprise discovered late is treated more seriously than a change reported early.

questions.prompt: Rohan receives a conditional offer, then a request for documents. He sends half of them and plans to send the rest later. What is the likely result?

options.text: The check cannot move forward on partial information, so his start is likely to slip until everything arrives
Nothing changes, because the checks team starts a clock only when the unconditional offer is issued
The department will approve the checks on the documents it has and collect the rest from him in his first month
His offer is withdrawn immediately, since a partial reply is treated in the same way as a false statement

questions.hint: A partial reply leaves the check incomplete, so the process waits for the rest.

questions.prompt: Which order best reflects the usual path to a start date?

options.text: Resign from your job as soon as you receive the letter, accept the offer, then supply the checks information once your notice period has started
Wait until the start date given in the advert arrives, then accept the offer and supply the checks information during that first week
Supply checks information, attend induction, then accept the offer once you have met the team
Accept the offer, supply checks information, vetting if needed, then written confirmation that you can start

questions.hint: Acceptance and checks come before confirmation of a start date; irreversible steps come last.

questions.prompt: The advert said the post would start in three months, but your checks team now says the date is not confirmed. Which source decides the date?

options.text: The advert, because it was the first public statement and the department is bound to it
The offer letter and the checks team, because the advert is only a guide
Your future line manager, who can agree any date directly with you whatever the checks say
Your current employer, whose notice period is the only date that matters for the department

questions.hint: Dates are confirmed by the department's offer correspondence, not the original advert.

questions.prompt: Imani's current contract needs three months' notice. The department wants her within a month. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Resign now and offer the department a start date after the notice, hoping that it will agree
Accept the one-month start date and plan to leave her current job without serving the notice
Explain her notice period to the recruiting team and ask whether a later start is possible, before she resigns
Ask her employer to waive the notice period, and say nothing to the department until it has agreed

questions.hint: Raise the constraint openly with the department first; do not resign on assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why are referees and past employers usually contacted in parallel with the other checks?

options.text: It allows the department to make a decision before the candidate has returned any forms
It saves time, because several strands of the process can proceed at once
It means that the candidate's own forms need not be checked against any other source
It is required by law that references are obtained before any other check starts

questions.hint: Parallel working shortens the elapsed time of the process.

questions.prompt: Which statement about asking the checks team a question is most accurate?

options.text: Questions should wait until the first day, when the person has full access to the team
Asking questions should be avoided, because candidates who ask are treated as less reliable
Asking when a request is unclear is better than guessing, because a wrong guess restarts the clock
Questions are answered only by the vetting service, which the candidate cannot contact

questions.hint: A short question avoids an incorrect answer that has to be redone.

questions.prompt: After accepting, Tomasz is offered a better job elsewhere. Which concern is most relevant to his decision?

options.text: He is legally bound to start in the Civil Service as soon as he accepts, whatever other options he may be given before the start date
He must not tell the Civil Service about the other job offer, or the department will withdraw its offer automatically and at once
He should accept both and decide on the day, because neither employer can check what he does
His offer is conditional and may never become final, so he should weigh the risk and be honest with both employers

questions.hint: A candidate who changes mind should tell the department promptly and honestly.

questions.prompt: The department confirms you can start with restricted access while clearance is pending. What does that mean for your first weeks?

options.text: You begin work but are kept away from material that needs the clearance, which may limit the tasks you are given
You must complete all mandatory learning before the restrictions are lifted
You may not enter the building until clearance arrives, so you cannot start in practice
You may see all material at the level required, because the clearance decision is treated as certain

questions.hint: Interim access limits what you can see, not whether you can start.

questions.prompt: Which action is most likely to cause avoidable delay?

options.text: Telling the checks team in advance that you will be abroad when a form is due
Completing the vetting questionnaire as soon as it arrives, with all attachments
Sending a scan with the wrong document type because the request was not read carefully
Asking the checks team which of two accepted documents they would prefer

questions.hint: Carelessness with requests creates repeat cycles; early notice and questions do not.

questions.prompt: Why should a change of circumstances, such as a new address, be reported before the start date?

options.text: Because the new address needs a fresh offer letter to be issued by the department
A late surprise is treated more seriously than a change reported early
Because the department pays travel costs based on the address at the time of the offer
Because addresses affect which department the person is allowed to join

questions.hint: Early reporting keeps the record accurate and shows openness.

items.title: L7: Spotting errors in a completed form
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; UK Security Vetting guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Checks teams spend much of their time finding the same few kinds of problem in forms, and knowing them helps you complete yours well. The most common are dates that do not join up, a name that differs from the identity documents, an address history with gaps, an employer named that cannot be traced, and answers to the same question that disagree in two places.

Dates matter because the employment history has to account for a continuous period. If one job ends in June and the next begins in September, the gap needs an explanation, even if it is short. If two jobs overlap, the overlap needs to be genuine and, if it is not obvious why, noted. Names matter because the check ties your documents together, so your form should use the name on your identity document, with other names listed as previous names. Addresses should show where you actually lived, with move-in and move-out dates.

Review your own form as a checker would. Read it once for dates, once for names, once for places and once for consistency of the story it tells. Ask whether every statement could be supported by a document or a person. If you find a mistake after submission, tell the team at once. A correction you volunteer is treated as honesty. The same correction found by the checker looks like an attempt to conceal.

Do not tidy a form to look better. A form that records a messy life accurately is better than a smooth one that cannot be supported.

questions.prompt: A form shows one job ending in June and the next starting in September, with no explanation. What is the likely response from the checker?

options.text: They will treat the form as false, because a gap of any length in the history is automatically disqualifying
They will fill the gap themselves from the applicant's tax records, without needing to ask the applicant anything
They will ignore it, because gaps of under six months never need to be explained on a baseline check
They will ask for an explanation of the gap, which is easy to give if the applicant has an honest answer

questions.hint: Gaps need an explanation, and a plain one is normally accepted.

questions.prompt: Tessa used on her form the name she prefers socially, not the one on her passport. What problem does this cause?

options.text: The form does not match the documents, so the checker cannot easily tie them to one identity
The form will be accepted, but she will be paid under the passport name only until she changes it
None, because the name used socially is the one that the department will record in any case
The department will amend her passport to match the form, as part of its own checks

questions.hint: The form should use the name on the identity documents, with other names listed as previous names.

questions.prompt: A candidate lists two full-time jobs for the same six months and says nothing. What should they have done?

options.text: Deleted the shorter job from the form, so that the history reads as one continuous line
Left the form as it is, because an overlap shows that the person is hardworking and in demand
Added a note explaining how the overlap arose, such as a handover or a part-time arrangement
Moved the start date of the second job forward, to remove the overlap from the dates

questions.hint: Unexplained overlaps invite questions; a short note settles them.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest sign that a form has been 'tidied' to look better than the facts?

options.text: A form listing several previous addresses over three years, each with dates
A form listing a former employer that has since closed, with other evidence
A history with one short gap that the applicant has explained and supported
A smooth history which no document or person can support

questions.hint: A smooth account that cannot be evidenced is more worrying than a messy true one.

questions.prompt: Elias spots a wrong date on his form the day after submitting it. What should he do?

options.text: Resubmit the whole form without any comment, so that nobody can tell which part of it was changed or when
Tell the checks team at once and give the right date, since a volunteered correction reads as honesty
Say nothing unless someone asks, because a single wrong date in a long form can never make any real difference
Wait to see whether the checker notices, so as not to draw attention to the form

questions.hint: A correction made promptly by the applicant is seen as honest; one found by the checker is not.

questions.prompt: Which approach best reflects reading your own form 'as a checker would'?

options.text: Read it once for dates, once for names, once for places and once for whether the story hangs together
Read it aloud to a friend, who can say whether it sounds convincing as a whole
Read only the sections that you changed since the last draft, since the rest has been checked
Read it once for spelling and punctuation, which are the most common causes of delay

questions.hint: Checkers look for dates, names, places and consistency, so check those deliberately.

questions.prompt: An applicant gives two different dates of birth, one on the form and one on a document, and says it was a typing error. What will the checker most likely do?

options.text: Ask for evidence of the correct date, and for the applicant to confirm it in writing
Refuse the application at once, because any difference in a birth date is treated as fraud
Accept the form date, because the applicant has said which one is right
Accept the document date, because documents always override whatever an applicant has written

questions.hint: A stated typing error still needs verifying against the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement about supporting evidence is most accurate?

options.text: Only the employment history needs evidence, and the other parts are taken on trust
Evidence is needed only when the department asks for it by name in the request
Evidence is needed for the most recent year only, since earlier dates are not checked
Every statement on the form should be one that a document or a person could support

questions.hint: The checks are built on being able to verify what you wrote.

questions.prompt: A former employer named on a form cannot be traced. What helps the checker most?

options.text: A blank entry, so that the employer is not mentioned at all on the form
Other evidence such as a contract, payslips, or a colleague who can confirm the work
An offer to explain the history in person to your line manager on the first day
A statement that the employer was well known and had a good reputation in its sector

questions.hint: Offer other evidence for the dates when the employer is gone.

questions.prompt: Why can a correction found by the checker look worse than the same correction volunteered by the applicant?

options.text: The department charges the applicant a fee for each correction that its own checkers find
Corrections found by checkers cannot be reversed in any later stage of the process
It looks as if the applicant hoped to conceal it, which is a question of honesty rather than accuracy
Corrections found by checkers must be treated as criminal offences under the rules

questions.hint: What counts is whether the applicant came forward or was caught.

items.title: L7: Awkward employment histories
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body:
Real working lives rarely fit a tidy box, and the employment check is designed to cope with that, as long as you describe your history honestly. Some cases come up repeatedly.

Agency and temporary work: you may have worked through an agency while being placed with several end clients. The agency is usually the employer for confirmation purposes, so name it and give the dates, adding the places where you worked if the form asks. Zero-hours and casual work: list the employer and the period over which you were on their books, even if you worked only occasionally. Self-employment and freelance work: list yourself as self-employed with the trading name, and give a client, accountant or tax record that can confirm it.

Redundancy and dismissal: the form usually asks why you left. Give the true reason in plain words. A dismissal does not automatically end a Civil Service career, but hiding it can. Career breaks: study, travel, caring, illness and parenting are all legitimate. State what the period was. Time overseas: give the country, the employer or institution if any, and the dates.

The principle is that the checker needs a continuous account, with someone or something that can support each part. If a period cannot be supported by a third party, say so and offer your own documents, such as a contract, payslip, tenancy agreement or travel record.

Never convert one kind of history into another to make it look better, for instance by describing a period of job-seeking as consultancy.

questions.prompt: Nell worked through an agency and was placed with three different companies in one year. Who should she name as the employer?

options.text: None of them, since temporary work does not have to be listed on a baseline history
The agency, with the dates, and the three clients too if the form asks for them
Whichever of the three clients she liked best, since it will give the most favourable reference
All three clients as separate employers, but not the agency, because the clients paid for the work

questions.hint: The agency is usually the employer for confirmation; add placements if asked.

questions.prompt: Mo had a zero-hours contract with a shop for two years and worked only a few shifts. How should he record it?

options.text: As employment over the period he was on their books, even though he worked few shifts
Not at all, because work on a zero-hours contract does not count as employment for the purposes of this particular check
As a single week of work, since a week is much closer to the amount of work that he actually did in practice
As self-employment, because he chose which shifts to accept

questions.hint: List the employer and the period over which you were on their books.

questions.prompt: Why does a department want the true reason for leaving a job?

options.text: The reason sets the pay band for the new role, according to how the last job ended
The reason is collected for statistics only and plays no part in any decision
A dismissal always stops the application, so the reason is what decides the outcome
It tests honesty and consistency, and an honestly given dismissal does not automatically end a Civil Service career

questions.hint: Honesty about the reason is what the checker values.

questions.prompt: A candidate was dismissed from a job and writes 'left to pursue other opportunities'. What is the main problem?

options.text: The problem is that the candidate should not have mentioned the job at all
The only problem is that the phrase is informal, so it should be reworded more formally
The statement is untrue, and a hidden dismissal can end the application when an honest one might not
There is no problem, because that phrase is the standard way to describe any departure

questions.hint: A false reason is dishonest, and dishonesty weighs more than the dismissal.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legitimate way to describe a career break?

options.text: As study, where the person occasionally read about their profession at home
As a period of caring, stating the dates and who can confirm it
As employment, where a relative paid for a little help given from time to time
As consultancy work, where the person spent part of the time looking for a job

questions.hint: State what the period was; do not turn one kind of history into another.

questions.prompt: Priya worked freelance as a translator. What should her form include to support the period?

options.text: Her job title only, because freelance work of this kind cannot be supported by any document or any person at all
A list of every client she has ever worked for since she started freelancing, whatever the year the work was done
A reference from a friend who has often seen her working at home and can describe what she did
Her trading name, and a client, accountant or tax record that can confirm the work

questions.hint: Self-employment needs a third party or records that can confirm it.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if no third party can confirm a period?

options.text: Ask a friend to write a letter confirming the period, even though the friend did not witness it
Invent a plausible employer, since the checker will not be able to disprove it
Say so, and offer their own documents such as a contract, payslips, tenancy agreement or travel record
Leave the period out, as unsupported periods are not counted by the department

questions.hint: Own documents help when no third party exists; invention never does.

questions.prompt: What information should time spent overseas be recorded with?

options.text: The country, the employer or institution if any, and the dates
Nothing, as overseas time is outside the scope of the check
The city only, as the country is obvious from the dates given
The country only, since the checker cannot ask overseas bodies for anything

questions.hint: Give enough detail that each part of the account is supportable.

questions.prompt: What is the principle that links all of these awkward cases?

options.text: The checker needs a continuous, honest account, with something to support each part
The checker wants a history that looks as conventional as possible
The checker wants evidence that the person has always had full-time employment
The checker wants the history in the shortest possible form

questions.hint: Continuity and support, not conventionality, are what matter.

questions.prompt: Why is describing a period of job-seeking as 'consultancy' a problem?

options.text: It is not a problem, since periods of self-employment cannot be checked
It turns one kind of history into another to look better, which is dishonest
It is acceptable if the person did one small piece of paid work during that period
It is helpful, since consultancy sounds more employable than job-seeking

questions.hint: Recasting history to look better is not allowed.

items.title: L7: Weighing a declared conviction
items.source: Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 (legislation.gov.uk); HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard
items.body:
When an applicant declares an unspent conviction, the department does not simply accept or reject. It looks at the facts and decides whether employing the person is appropriate for that role. Factors that are commonly weighed include the nature of the offence, how long ago it happened, the sentence, the applicant's age at the time, what has happened since, and whether the offence is relevant to the duties of the role. A fraud conviction matters more for a role handling money than for a role in policy analysis, though both are considered.

The applicant's honesty carries heavy weight. A full, early and accurate declaration, with a short plain explanation, is treated much better than a partial one. A declaration that is later found to be understated, for example a declared caution that was in fact a conviction, undermines trust.

The form tells you what is being asked. For most posts the question concerns unspent convictions; for roles exempt from the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act, it can also cover spent ones. Either way, you answer what is asked, in the terms in which it is asked. If you are unsure whether a matter is covered, ask the checks team instead of choosing the answer that looks safest.

A declaration is confidential. The information goes to those who need it for the decision, and it is held under data protection rules. An applicant who is refused can ask for the reasons and use the department's process to challenge the decision. Equality law protects people from discrimination on the grounds of protected characteristics, though a conviction itself is not one of them.

The lesson is that the process is a judgement about suitability and trust, not an automatic bar.

questions.prompt: Which pair of facts would make an unspent conviction most relevant to a particular role?

options.text: The offence took place when the applicant was a young adult and led to a modest sentence
The offence was a minor driving matter, and the post has no driving duties of any kind
The offence is old and unrelated to the work, and the person has had no trouble since it happened
The offence is recent and directly connected to the duties, such as fraud for a post handling money

questions.hint: Relevance to the duties and recency both increase the weight given to a conviction.

questions.prompt: Why is a full early declaration treated better than a partial one?

options.text: A partial declaration is treated as a spent conviction, which then cannot be taken into account
The rehabilitation rules automatically refuse any declaration that is shorter than the form allows
Honesty carries heavy weight, and a partial declaration can suggest that the rest is being held back
The department scores applications by length, so a long declaration earns more marks than a short one

questions.hint: The same facts look different when volunteered completely.

questions.prompt: An applicant declares a caution, but the record shows a conviction. How is this likely to be seen?

options.text: As irrelevant, because the department decides only on convictions that appear in the form's own wording
As a harmless difference in wording, because in law a caution and a conviction are the same thing
As an understatement that damages trust, on top of the offence itself
As evidence of honesty, because the applicant declared something rather than nothing

questions.hint: Understating undermines the credibility of the whole declaration.

questions.prompt: The form asks only about unspent convictions. Alan is unsure whether an old matter is unspent. What is the best step?

options.text: Ask the checks team, or check the rehabilitation rules, before he answers
Answer that there is nothing to declare, on the basis that a doubtful matter is probably spent
Describe it in vague terms, so that his answer is true whichever way the rules are read
Leave the question blank and see whether the team chases him for an answer

questions.hint: Ask rather than guess; do not answer ambiguously.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the confidentiality of a declaration is most accurate?

options.text: It is kept on a public register of applicants, which anyone can search
It is added to the department's internal staff directory so that the new team knows in advance
It is shared with the applicant's current employer so that they can comment on the circumstances
The information goes to those who need it for the decision and is held under data protection rules

questions.hint: Declarations are handled confidentially and shared only as needed.

questions.prompt: After a refusal, Sam believes the decision was unfair. What can Sam do?

options.text: Accept the decision at once, since refusals in the Civil Service cannot be challenged
Ask for the reasons and use the department's process to challenge the decision
Contact the person who handled the form at home and argue for a reversal
Reapply the next day with the same form, since the second decision will be made by someone else

questions.hint: Challenge routes exist and reasons can be requested.

questions.prompt: Which statement about discrimination law and convictions is correct?

options.text: Equality law protects protected characteristics, but a conviction is not itself one of them
Equality law applies only to recruitment and not to people already employed
Equality law forbids any question about convictions at any stage of recruitment
A conviction is a protected characteristic, so it can never be taken into account in a decision

questions.hint: Convictions are not protected characteristics, though the process must still be fair.

questions.prompt: A role is exempt from the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act. What can the form ask?

options.text: It can ask only about unspent convictions, as for any other post
It can ask only about convictions from the previous year
It can ask about spent convictions as well as unspent ones
It can ask nothing about convictions, because exemption removes such questions

questions.hint: Exemption allows questions about spent convictions.

questions.prompt: What is the key message about how declarations are decided?

options.text: It is an automatic bar, with exceptions only for minor offences
It is a judgement about suitability and trust, not an automatic bar
It is decided on the sentence alone, ignoring every other fact
It is decided by the applicant's referees rather than the department

questions.hint: The decision weighs context; it is not mechanical.

questions.prompt: Why does the age of the applicant at the time of an offence matter?

options.text: It decides the pay band of the posts that the person may apply for
It decides how long the conviction stays on a public register
It makes the conviction spent on the person's next birthday
It forms part of the context, along with what has happened since

questions.hint: Age at the time is one factor in weighing the context.

items.title: L7: Right to work and nationality in realistic cases
items.source: GOV.UK: Check a job applicant's right to work; Civil Service Nationality Rules
items.body:
Right to work checks and nationality rules are often confused, so it helps to separate the questions they answer. The right to work check asks whether the law allows this person to work for this employer. The nationality rules ask whether this post is open to people of this status. Both must be satisfied, and clearance is a third matter.

In practice, the employer carries out the right to work check before employment starts, and keeps a dated record. The method depends on the evidence: a British or Irish passport can be checked in person or through an approved digital service, while someone with immigration permission typically provides a share code so the employer can view the status online. Where permission has an end date, the employer diarises a follow-up check before it ends. If the person has applied to extend in time, the employer follows Home Office guidance instead of assuming either way.

Nationality matters for eligibility and may change over time. Someone who becomes a British citizen while employed should update their records so that the department holds the right information. Moving to another post or department can bring new eligibility questions, because a different post may have a narrower statement.

Agency workers and contractors raise their own questions. The agency or contractor may do the right to work check, and the department's rules on access and clearance still apply to the work. A department cannot waive its own security requirements because someone else has done a check.

When in doubt, ask the person responsible for resourcing, not a colleague.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly separates the two questions?

options.text: Right to work is carried out by the Home Office; nationality rules are carried out by the employer
Right to work asks whether the law allows the person to work; nationality rules ask whether the post is open to people of that status
Right to work asks about the person's loyalty; nationality rules ask about their qualifications
Right to work applies to the first job only; nationality rules apply to later jobs

questions.hint: They answer different questions and both must be met.

questions.prompt: Maya has indefinite permission to work, but the advert is for UK nationals only. What is her position?

options.text: She is eligible, because the right to work always satisfies a nationality statement
She is eligible if her manager agrees, since a manager can waive the statement
She is eligible if she has worked in the Civil Service before this advert
She has the right to work but is not eligible for this post

questions.hint: Having the right to work does not satisfy a UK-only statement.

questions.prompt: The employer views a share code for a new starter whose permission ends in nine months. What should it diarise?

options.text: A follow-up check before the permission ends
A request for the person to leave before the end date
A request for a fresh security questionnaire from the person
Nothing, since the first check covers the whole period of employment

questions.hint: Time-limited permission needs a follow-up check.

questions.prompt: A new starter becomes a British citizen during employment. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Resign and rejoin, because the original appointment was made on a different basis
Reapply for the job as a UK national, since the first appointment no longer applies
Update the department's records so that it holds the correct information
Say nothing, because a change of citizenship never matters to an employer

questions.hint: Records should be accurate when status changes.

questions.prompt: Why might moving to another post cause a new eligibility question?

options.text: The old post's eligibility transfers only for the first month after the move
The new post may have a narrower eligibility statement than the old one
The new post is always at a lower grade, and so has different rules
The right to work must be rechecked at every move between posts

questions.hint: Different posts can have different statements.

questions.prompt: An agency supplies a contractor who has passed the agency's right to work check. What still applies?

options.text: The department's own security and clearance rules for the work
Only the right to work check, repeated by the department
Nothing, because the agency has dealt with every check that the department could ask for
Only the nationality rules, as clearance is never needed for contractors

questions.hint: A check by someone else does not remove the department's own requirements.

questions.prompt: Who should you ask if you are unsure about an applicant's eligibility?

options.text: The applicant's previous manager, who knows the person's circumstances
A friend in another department, who may have dealt with the same question
The person responsible for resourcing, or the contact in the advert
A colleague who joined from a similar background and so will know the rules

questions.hint: Ask the responsible person, not whoever is nearby.

questions.prompt: What should the employer do when someone has applied in time to extend permission?

options.text: Stop work immediately, because the permission is about to end
Ask the person to arrange a check with their previous employer
Continue as normal with no checks, because an application is the same as permission
Follow Home Office guidance for that situation rather than assuming either way

questions.hint: Official guidance sets out what applies.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a record the employer typically keeps?

options.text: The employee's full immigration history over the past ten years
A photograph of the employee's home address
A dated copy of the right to work check, held securely
A signed statement from the employee's family

questions.hint: The employer keeps evidence that the check was done correctly.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to assume that being cleared to work means being cleared for the post?

options.text: Right to work, nationality rules and clearance are separate matters, and each must be satisfied
Because the right to work is normally revoked at the moment the person is appointed to the post
Because the pay band of the post decides who is cleared for it, so the lower grades need no other test
Because the right to work is simply a temporary form of clearance that lasts until a vetting decision is made

questions.hint: Different requirements answer different questions.

items.title: L7: Classification, aggregation and need to know
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy (GOV.UK); Cabinet Office guidance on security
items.body:
Classification is about the harm if information is compromised, but it is not applied to each fact in isolation. Aggregation matters: a large collection of individually low-risk information can be more sensitive than any single item. A spreadsheet containing the names and addresses of thousands of people may be OFFICIAL, yet its loss could do real harm, so it is handled with extra care, often marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, and accessed only by those who need it.

This is why clearance level does not follow only the classification of each document. A role that regularly works with large datasets, or that holds the keys to systems, may need a higher level than the classification of any single document suggests. The sponsor looks at what the role can reach and what harm a malicious or careless holder could do.

Need to know is the second control. Even where a person has the right clearance and works in the same team, they should see only what their work requires. This limits damage from error, from curiosity and from a compromised account. It also protects the person, because a pattern of looking at things outside your work can be investigated as misuse.

Markings guide handling, but they do not replace judgement. Unmarked information can still be sensitive. If you are unsure, treat it with care and ask the owner, who sets the classification.

When sharing, apply the minimum: the minimum information, to the minimum people, for the minimum time, by an approved route. If something is marked incorrectly, tell the owner so that it can be corrected rather than quietly ignoring the mark.

questions.prompt: Why can a spreadsheet of thousands of names and addresses need more careful handling than a single name and address?

options.text: Spreadsheets are always classified one level higher than letters carrying the same information
Aggregation: a large collection can cause more harm if lost than any single item in it
Larger files take longer to send, and the delay itself creates the extra security risk
Names and addresses become TOP SECRET once more than a few dozen are held together

questions.hint: Collections can be more sensitive than their parts.

questions.prompt: A role maintains a database holding the data of many people but reads none of it. Which view is most sensible?

options.text: The role needs only baseline checks, because the person reads no data
The role needs no checks, because a database is a system and not information
The role needs DV, as anyone with access to a database holds TOP SECRET material
The role's reach and the harm it could cause may justify a higher clearance than any single record suggests

questions.hint: Clearance reflects what the role can reach, not only what it reads.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of need to know even among people who hold the right clearance?

options.text: It makes the clearance process quicker, because fewer checks are needed
It limits the damage from error, curiosity or a compromised account
It lets managers decide for themselves who among their staff is trusted
It means that fewer people need to be given clearance in the first place

questions.hint: The control reduces exposure inside cleared groups.

questions.prompt: How can looking at records outside your work cause a problem for you personally?

options.text: It makes your manager personally responsible for whatever records you happened to see
It has no consequences where the records are only OFFICIAL
A pattern of such access can be investigated as misuse, even if the motive was innocent curiosity
It lowers your clearance level automatically at the end of the month in which it happens

questions.hint: Unneeded access leaves an audit trail and can be treated as misuse.

questions.prompt: You think a document is unmarked but sensitive. What is the best step?

options.text: Mark it TOP SECRET yourself, to be on the safe side
Treat it as public, because it carries no marking and so is not protected
Delete it so that it cannot be misused by anyone who finds it
Treat it with care and ask the owner, who sets the classification

questions.hint: Markings guide handling, but judgement fills the gaps.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the idea of 'minimum' when sharing information?

options.text: The minimum information, to the minimum people, for the minimum time, by an approved route
The lowest classification that the author can reasonably justify for the document in question and its contents
The minimum level of seniority that a recipient needs to have in order to be able to read the document
The smallest number of words that can be put in the covering email which goes out with the document

questions.hint: The principle limits the information, the audience and the time.

questions.prompt: You notice a document marked lower than its contents deserve. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it, since the marking is the owner's choice and cannot be questioned
Share it widely so that more people can judge the marking for themselves
Change the marking yourself, because you can see that it is wrong
Tell the owner so that the marking can be corrected

questions.hint: Report to the owner rather than ignore or alter.

questions.prompt: Why does a sponsor look at what a role can reach, rather than only the classification of documents?

options.text: Clearance is given for the document and not for the role that handles it
Sponsors prefer higher levels to lower ones, as they are safer to request
The harm a careless or malicious holder could do depends on reach as well as content
The classification of documents is never reliable enough to base a decision on

questions.hint: Role reach drives risk.

questions.prompt: Which action is most consistent with aggregation concerns?

options.text: Sending an extract with only the fields the recipient needs, instead of the whole dataset
Sending the whole dataset with a covering note saying which parts are relevant
Sending the dataset to a personal email address so it can be opened later at home
Splitting the dataset in two and sending both halves to the same person

questions.hint: Minimise the amount of data in any share.

questions.prompt: Does the fact that something is OFFICIAL mean it can be freely discussed?

options.text: Once the person has passed baseline checks, OFFICIAL material can be freely discussed
OFFICIAL still carries handling expectations and need to know applies
OFFICIAL material can be freely discussed provided the conversation is in a private home
OFFICIAL is the lowest level and so carries no restrictions at all

questions.hint: OFFICIAL is not public; handling still applies.

items.title: L7: Working remotely and in public
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; NCSC guidance for remote working (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Hybrid and remote working change where information is handled, not the rules for protecting it. The same expectations apply at home, on the train or in a cafe: work on approved devices, use approved systems, keep sensitive material out of sight and earshot, and report problems quickly.

At home, think about who else can see or hear your screen. Position the screen away from windows and shared spaces, use headphones for calls, lock the device when you step away and keep any paper in a place others cannot reach. Do not use personal email or personal cloud storage for official work, and do not photograph the screen with a personal phone. If a smart speaker or assistant is in the room, consider whether it should be there during sensitive calls, because it may be listening.

In public, the risk of being overheard or overlooked is higher. Avoid discussing sensitive matters or working on sensitive material in public spaces. Use a privacy screen if you must work on a train, and do not leave devices unattended for even a moment. Public Wi-Fi is not appropriate for official work unless it is through an approved secure connection.

When travelling abroad with a work device, follow your department's rules. Many departments restrict travel with devices to some countries, or require advance approval, because of the risks of theft and interference.

If you lose a device, or think it has been stolen or tampered with, report it at once through the security route. The first hour is the most valuable for limiting harm, and a prompt report is treated as responsible behaviour, not a failure.

questions.prompt: You need to take a call involving personal data while working from the kitchen table. What is the most sensible precaution?

options.text: Use headphones, keep the screen away from windows and other people, and check who can hear
Work exactly as normal, since your home is a private place and no one else in the house can overhear or see
Hold the call on speaker so that you can type your notes at the same time as the other person is talking
Hold the call on your own mobile phone, so that the work systems and work devices are not involved at all

questions.hint: Think about who can see and hear in a shared space.

questions.prompt: Which of these is not appropriate for official work?

options.text: Keeping paper where other people in the house cannot reach it
Saving a draft to a personal cloud storage account because it is easier to reach
Using an approved system through an approved device
Locking the laptop when you step into the next room

questions.hint: Personal cloud storage is not approved for official work.

questions.prompt: A colleague suggests photographing a screen with a personal phone to send a table to a friend. Why is this wrong?

options.text: It is allowed only when the table is classified above OFFICIAL
It is acceptable if the photograph is deleted after an hour
It is acceptable if the friend is also a civil servant
It takes official information outside approved systems and may expose it to others

questions.hint: Official information should stay on approved devices and systems.

questions.prompt: You must work on a train. What is the best response?

options.text: Use the train's public Wi-Fi, as it is faster than a mobile connection
Leave the laptop on the seat while you buy a coffee, as it is locked
Avoid sensitive material or use a privacy screen, and never leave the device unattended
Work as normal on any material, because train passengers are strangers and do not matter

questions.hint: Public places increase the chance of being overlooked or overheard.

questions.prompt: Why is public Wi-Fi a concern?

options.text: It is available only to private companies and so is not designed for use by people who work for the government
Others on the network may be able to intercept traffic unless an approved secure connection is used
It is always slower than other connections, which makes errors more likely in documents that are saved
It stops work from being saved to the department's systems, so documents are lost once the session ends

questions.hint: Unsecured networks can expose data in transit.

questions.prompt: Which statement about taking a work device abroad is most accurate?

options.text: Many departments restrict or require approval for travel with devices, to some countries in particular
Only mobile phones are restricted, not laptops
Devices can be taken anywhere so long as you tell your family where you are going
There are no restrictions, because all work devices are encrypted

questions.hint: Follow the department's rules before travelling.

questions.prompt: You think your laptop has been stolen from your car. What should you do first?

options.text: Wait a day in case it turns up, so as not to cause alarm
Report it only if you find evidence of damage to the car
Report it at once through the security route, even if you are not certain
Try to track it down yourself before telling anyone

questions.hint: The first hour is the most valuable for limiting harm.

questions.prompt: How is a prompt report of a lost device treated?

options.text: As proof that the device was not properly encrypted
As unnecessary, because lost devices are protected anyway
As an admission of negligence that will always be punished
As responsible behaviour, not a failure

questions.hint: Prompt reporting is encouraged.

questions.prompt: Why might a smart speaker matter during a sensitive call at home?

options.text: It may be listening and could capture what is said
It can be used to share the call with colleagues who are not in the meeting
It improves the quality of the call when it is placed nearby
It makes the call unlawful under data protection rules

questions.hint: Devices that listen are a risk to confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Which habit best protects a device when you step away for a moment?

options.text: Leave it open, since you will be back in a minute
Put a note next to it saying 'back soon'
Lock it, even for a short time
Turn the screen to face the wall

questions.hint: Locking is a simple, reliable habit.

items.title: L7: How a vetting application moves and what can go wrong
items.source: UK Security Vetting guidance; HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK)
items.body:
A vetting application has a clear sequence. The employing department decides that the role needs clearance and sponsors the applicant. The vetting service then sends the applicant a questionnaire and, depending on the level, gathers information from records, referees and the applicant. A vetting officer assesses it against published principles and reaches a recommendation; a decision follows. If clearance is granted, it is recorded for a particular role and level, and the holder takes on responsibilities: to report significant changes, to follow security rules, and to take part in reviews. This continuing work is called aftercare.

Things go wrong in predictable ways. The most common is an incomplete or inaccurate questionnaire, which is returned and delays everything. Another is unreachable referees, who must be given warning. A third is a late disclosure: something that comes out during the process but was not on the form. The vetting officer's concern is not only the fact but the failure to declare it. Another is a long gap in checkable history, such as years abroad without records, which can make it difficult to reach a decision and may lead to a refusal or to a lower-level clearance for the role.

If the outcome is unfavourable, the applicant can usually ask for the reasons, subject to what may be disclosed, and there is a formal route to challenge a refusal or withdrawal. The sponsoring department decides what to do about the job in the meantime, which may include moving the person to a role that needs no clearance.

Vetting does not look for perfection. It looks for honesty, reliability and resilience to pressure, and it expects that real lives include setbacks.

questions.prompt: Who decides that a role needs clearance, and who carries out the vetting?

options.text: The applicant's referees decide what the role needs, and the vetting service signs it off
The employing department sponsors the clearance, and the vetting service carries out the process
The vetting service decides which roles need clearance, and the department carries out the checks
The applicant decides what the role needs, and the department grants it on request

questions.hint: Sponsor and vetting service have different jobs.

questions.prompt: An applicant leaves out a debt, and the vetting officer finds it in the records. What is the main concern?

options.text: The fact that the debt is older than the questionnaire's cut-off date
The fact that the records were consulted without the applicant's specific permission
The size of the debt, which always decides the outcome by itself
The failure to declare it, as well as the debt itself

questions.hint: Late disclosure is judged as an honesty issue.

questions.prompt: Why might a long gap in checkable history cause difficulty?

options.text: Clearance is never given where there are any gaps in the checkable history, so the application must always be refused outright
Gaps in checkable history make the person ineligible for the right to work in the UK under the immigration rules
Any gap in checkable history is read as proof of dishonesty and ends the process
There may be too little to verify, which can limit what the vetting officer is able to decide

questions.hint: If there is too little to verify, assurance may be limited.

questions.prompt: What is meant by 'aftercare' for a person who holds clearance?

options.text: A support service for people who have been refused clearance
The continuing responsibilities of a clearance holder, including reporting significant changes and taking part in reviews
A medical check offered to staff once clearance has been granted
A repeat of the original questionnaire in the first week of the new job

questions.hint: Clearance does not end on approval; it continues with responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Which of these changes should someone with clearance usually report?

options.text: A new partner who is going to live with them, or a serious financial difficulty
A change of broadband provider at home, since it may affect their connection
A change of gym membership, since it may involve meeting new people
A change of hairdresser, since the person may be seen in a different place

questions.hint: Significant personal changes relevant to risk are reported.

questions.prompt: If a vetting application is refused, what is usually true?

options.text: The applicant must resign from the department straight away and has no right to ask any questions about the decision
The decision is final, and no information about the reasons for it can be requested by the applicant
The applicant can ask for the reasons, subject to what may be disclosed, and a formal route to challenge exists
The applicant can never apply for any government job again, whatever the circumstances or the passage of time

questions.hint: There are routes to understand and challenge.

questions.prompt: What might the sponsoring department do about the job while a challenge is pending?

options.text: Treat the clearance as granted until the whole process is finished
Ask the vetting service to make the decision again within a day
Decide how to handle the post, which may include placing the person in a role that needs no clearance
Remove the person from the Civil Service at once, as the vetting decision requires

questions.hint: The department manages the job separately from the vetting decision.

questions.prompt: Unreachable referees most often cause which problem?

options.text: Delay, because the process waits until they respond
Loss of the right to work, because the referees confirm status
A downgrade to baseline checks, which need no referees
Automatic refusal of clearance on the grounds of incomplete evidence

questions.hint: Referees who are not warned slow the process.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures what vetting looks for?

options.text: A record that matches the typical profile of a civil servant
A person who has never been in debt, in dispute or under any kind of strain
A life free of every mistake, since any past error shows poor judgement
Honesty, reliability and resilience to pressure, accepting that real lives include setbacks

questions.hint: Vetting tests trust and risk, not perfection.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful thing an applicant can do when something awkward is in their history?

options.text: Wait until clearance has been granted and then bring it up with the line manager
Declare it clearly with a short explanation before it is found
Hope it is not in the records and say nothing, since it may never be found
Mention it to a referee in the hope that it will be passed on informally

questions.hint: Volunteer early; concealment is the larger risk.

items.title: L7: Money, relationships and foreign links in vetting
items.source: UK Security Vetting guidance; HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Vetting looks at areas of life where a person could be put under pressure or be tempted to do something they should not. Three are especially common: money, relationships and foreign links.

Money: the concern is not wealth. It is whether financial difficulty, unmanageable debt, gambling or lavish spending unexplained by income could make someone open to bribery or blackmail. Ordinary debts such as a mortgage or a credit card balance that is being managed are normal. The key is to be open about them, and to show that you are dealing with them. Hiding a problem is a bigger worry than the problem.

Relationships: vetting at higher levels may ask about a partner and close family, and about close associates. This is not to judge anyone's choices. It is because someone close to you might be a route to pressure, or might themselves present a risk. Your partner may be asked to give some information, and you should explain this to them beforehand.

Foreign links: having family abroad, working overseas, holding another nationality or travelling widely is not a bar. Vetting wants to understand the links, particularly where a country poses a risk to UK interests or where someone could be pressured through relatives. Be open about the facts and about any contact with foreign officials or organisations.

Vetting does not discriminate on the basis of protected characteristics, and no particular background automatically rules a person out. Disclosure of sensitive personal matters is handled in confidence.

After clearance, significant changes in these areas, such as a new relationship, a serious debt, or new foreign contacts, are reported as part of aftercare.

questions.prompt: Why does vetting ask about debts and spending?

options.text: To decide the grade that the person will be offered in the new role, according to how their finances look
To judge whether the person is wealthy enough to be given a post at that level of seniority in government
To judge whether financial pressure could make someone open to bribery or blackmail
To decide whether the person can afford to meet the cost of the clearance process out of their own money

questions.hint: The concern is vulnerability, not wealth.

questions.prompt: Which attitude to a credit card balance that is being managed is right?

options.text: It is normal and should be declared openly, with the position explained
It must be repaid in full before applying, or the application will fail
It must be hidden, because any debt is a bar to clearance at every level
It is irrelevant to vetting, so it should not appear on any form

questions.hint: Ordinary managed debt is not a bar; concealment is the risk.

questions.prompt: Why might a vetting form ask about a partner?

options.text: To decide whether the partner can apply for the same job in the same team
To establish who will receive the pension if the applicant dies in service
To check that the person is married, since marriage is a condition of clearance
Someone close could be a route to pressure or present a risk, and it is not a judgement on the person's choices

questions.hint: The questions concern risk, not lifestyle.

questions.prompt: Before information about a partner is given, what should the applicant do?

options.text: Leave the partner out of the form altogether so the partner is not troubled
Explain to the partner what is being asked and why
Say nothing, because the partner will never be asked for anything
Ask the partner to apply for clearance as well, to keep the record balanced

questions.hint: The partner may be asked to give information, so should be told.

questions.prompt: Does holding another nationality automatically stop someone being cleared?

options.text: It does, in every case and at every level of clearance
It does not, and it is never considered by the vetting officer
It does at DV level only, since lower levels never ask about nationality
It does not, but the links are considered, especially where there is a risk to UK interests

questions.hint: Foreign links are looked at, not banned.

questions.prompt: Which is the right approach to contact with foreign officials?

options.text: Be open about the facts on the form and as part of aftercare
Mention it only to a family member who can pass it on
Wait until after clearance is granted before saying anything
Leave it out unless asked about it at an interview

questions.hint: Openness about contacts is expected.

questions.prompt: How is the disclosure of sensitive personal matters handled in vetting?

options.text: It is published within the department so that colleagues know the position
In confidence, and no particular background automatically rules a person out
It is used only to decide the person's pay and any allowances that go with the role
It is passed to the person's line manager for them to act on

questions.hint: Vetting is confidential and non-discriminatory.

questions.prompt: After clearance, you form a new close relationship with someone from abroad. What should you do?

options.text: Wait to be asked at the next review, which is the proper time to raise it
End the relationship to avoid a problem with clearance
Report it as a significant change, as part of aftercare
Say nothing, because personal relationships are private and not a matter for the employer

questions.hint: Significant personal changes are reported.

questions.prompt: Which of these would be of most concern in the financial part of vetting?

options.text: A student loan that is being repaid on schedule
Spending well beyond known income with no explanation, or gambling that is out of control
A credit card balance that is cleared every month
A mortgage taken out to buy a first home

questions.hint: Unexplained spending and unmanaged problems create vulnerability.

questions.prompt: What is the main message about disclosing a problem in these areas?

options.text: Being open and showing that it is being dealt with counts for much more than the problem itself
Problems should be disclosed only to the line manager, who can decide what to do
Problems stop being relevant after the first year of employment
Problems should be kept off the form until they are solved, so that the form looks clean

questions.hint: Openness reduces vulnerability.

items.title: L7: Speaking about work: friends, social media and FOI
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; Civil Service Code; Freedom of Information Act 2000 (legislation.gov.uk)
items.body:
Civil servants may talk about their work in general terms, but they owe confidentiality about official information they hold because of their job. The Civil Service Code requires integrity and objectivity, and Civil Service Management Code rules limit public comment on policy and political matters. For social media the same expectations apply as in any public setting: you are identifiable as a civil servant, whether or not you say so, and posts can be seen by colleagues, journalists and the public.

Practical guidance: do not post anything about internal discussions, unreleased decisions or colleagues' personal details. Do not use your official role to promote personal views. If you identify as a civil servant online, make clear the views are your own, but remember that does not make an improper comment acceptable. Keep personal accounts private and review who can see them. If you see something online about your department that is wrong or damaging, do not reply as if you were speaking for it; refer it to the press office.

The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives the public a right to request information held by public authorities. Individual staff do not decide on these requests. If you receive one, send it promptly to the team that handles them; the authority has a limited time, normally 20 working days, to respond. Do not delete or alter information once a request has been received, because that can be an offence.

Disclosure of protected information under the Official Secrets Act can be a criminal offence, and the duty continues after you leave.

When in doubt, ask your line manager or the press office before you speak or post.

questions.prompt: You post on a personal account that you are a civil servant, and share a view on a policy your department works on. What is the best assessment?

options.text: It is fine, because a personal account is private to the owner whatever the account says and whoever may read it
It is fine as long as you add the words 'views my own' to your profile, which makes it clear you speak only for yourself
You are identifiable as a civil servant, so the post may reflect on the department and could breach the rules on public comment
It is fine so long as you do not mention the name of the department anywhere on the account or in the post itself

questions.hint: Identification as a civil servant brings expectations whatever the disclaimer.

questions.prompt: Which of these is it never appropriate to post?

options.text: A link to a press release that the department has published
A congratulation to a colleague on a published report
A photograph of your lunch taken at your desk
Details of internal discussions or decisions not yet released

questions.hint: Internal matters should not be disclosed.

questions.prompt: You see a post criticising your department that contains a factual error. What is the best step?

options.text: Send the poster a private message pointing out the error
Reply with the correction, since you know the facts better than anyone
Refer it to the press office rather than replying as if you spoke for the department
Ignore it and report the poster to the police for defamation

questions.hint: Corrections go through those authorised to speak.

questions.prompt: A member of the public emails you a request for information about how a decision was made. What should you do?

options.text: Answer it yourself straight away, as you know the facts and a quick personal reply is more helpful than a formal one
Delete it, because the request was not addressed to the right person and so does not count as a request to the department
Forward it to a friend in the press office, who can deal with it informally and more quickly than the formal team
Send it promptly to the team that handles Freedom of Information requests

questions.hint: Requests are handled by the specialist team.

questions.prompt: How long does a public authority normally have to respond to an FOI request?

options.text: There is no time limit at all
20 working days
6 months
2 working days

questions.hint: The normal limit is 20 working days.

questions.prompt: After receiving an FOI request, you discover an old email that would be embarrassing. What must you not do?

options.text: Delete or alter it, because that can be an offence once a request has been received
Mention it to your manager so they are aware of it
Leave it where it is stored on the system
Hand it to the FOI team with the rest of the information

questions.hint: Information must be preserved once a request is received.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Official Secrets Act and social media is correct?

options.text: Posting protected information could be an offence, and the duty continues after leaving
It does not apply to anonymous accounts
It applies only to articles printed in newspapers
It applies only while you are at work

questions.hint: The law covers any unauthorised disclosure in any medium.

questions.prompt: Why does 'views my own' not make every comment acceptable?

options.text: It is valid only on an official account that is run by the department and not on a personal one
It makes the comments legally protected, so that no complaint can be made about them to the department
It does not remove the duty of confidentiality or the expectation of impartiality
It applies only to posts about political matters, and not to posts that are about your own work or colleagues

questions.hint: A disclaimer does not override duties.

questions.prompt: What is the safest default when you are unsure whether you may speak or post about something?

options.text: Post it on a private account that only friends can see
Ask your line manager or the press office first
Mention it to friends first and see what they think
Post it and delete it if there are complaints

questions.hint: Ask before, not after.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a general-terms description of your work that is normally fine?

options.text: 'We are about to change the rules for a benefit next month'
'My manager is under investigation for how she handled a case'
'This week we found a security fault in one of our systems'
'I work in a team that deals with customer enquiries'

questions.hint: Describing your role in general terms is fine.

items.title: L7: Leaving, gifts and outside interests in detail
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Code; Bribery Act 2010
items.body:
The rules on gifts, hospitality and outside interests follow a simple idea: public servants must not be, or appear to be, influenced by private benefit. The detail is set by each department, but common patterns exist.

Gifts and hospitality: items of low value, such as a branded pen or modest refreshments at a meeting, may be accepted under local rules. Even then they may be recorded. Anything that could look like a reward or inducement, particularly from a supplier in a live process, a regulated body or someone seeking a decision, should be declined and the offer recorded. Cash and gift cards are never acceptable. Hospitality that is lavish, repeated or not linked to work is a warning sign. If you are not sure, ask a manager before you accept.

Outside interests: second jobs, directorships, voluntary roles, investments and a family member's business may need to be declared, and some require approval. The test is whether the interest could conflict with your duties, take time from them, or use official information.

Political activity is graded: staff in the most junior and non-public-facing roles have greater freedom, while senior and sensitive roles are the most restricted and may need permission to take part in national politics.

When leaving: rules on business appointments apply to people who leave and take up work in the private sector, particularly where they dealt with that organisation or hold sensitive knowledge. Senior leavers may need advice from an independent committee. Even if rules do not strictly apply, you must not use official information for the benefit of a new employer.

Declaring early lets the department manage a situation and protects you.

questions.prompt: A supplier invites you to a lavish dinner while a tender is live. What is the correct response?

options.text: Accept if you pay for your own taxi home, so that the supplier bears only the cost of the meal
Decline it and record the offer
Accept if you bring a colleague with you, so that there is a witness to the conversation
Accept if you promise not to discuss the tender, since the invitation is then purely social

questions.hint: Hospitality from a supplier in a live process should be declined and recorded.

questions.prompt: Which gift would normally be unacceptable under any department's rules?

options.text: Tea and biscuits provided during a long meeting at a supplier's office
A box of chocolates left for the whole team at the end of a project
A branded pen handed out to everyone attending a supplier meeting
A gift card of any value

questions.hint: Cash and gift cards are never acceptable.

questions.prompt: Your sibling sets up a business that sells to your department's sector. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Declare the interest so the department can decide whether it needs managing
Resign from your post, since any family link with the sector is an automatic bar to employment
Say nothing, because you have no financial stake in the business and nothing to gain
Ask your sibling to avoid your department, so that no conflict can arise in practice

questions.hint: The test is whether it could appear to conflict, so declare it.

questions.prompt: Which test best describes when an outside interest is a problem?

options.text: It earns you money, since the rules forbid any paid work outside the Civil Service
It takes place at a weekend, when the department is unable to supervise it
It could conflict with your duties, take time from them, or involve using official information
It involves other people, since outside activity must always be done alone

questions.hint: The focus is conflict, time and misuse of information.

questions.prompt: How are political activity rules usually graded?

options.text: The same for every grade, with no distinction between one role and another
Restrictions fall on the most junior staff, who are the least able to speak for the department
Restrictions apply only during an election period, when political activity is at its highest
More freedom for junior non-public-facing roles, with senior and sensitive roles the most restricted

questions.hint: The Code grades restrictions by role.

questions.prompt: You are leaving to join a company that your team regulates. What is the right thing to do?

options.text: Delay announcing it until you start work there, to avoid a conflict with your notice period
Check the business appointment rules and seek advice before you accept
Accept and tell your manager on your last day, once the move is settled
Accept and say nothing, since you will have left by the time that anyone notices

questions.hint: Rules on business appointments can apply to leavers.

questions.prompt: Even where the business appointment rules do not strictly apply, what must a leaver never do?

options.text: Mention the former post on a CV or in an interview
Attend a trade event in their own time as a private person
Use official information for the benefit of a new employer
Keep in touch with former colleagues in a personal capacity

questions.hint: Misuse of information is wrong whenever you leave.

questions.prompt: A supplier sends a modest hamper at the end of a completed contract. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Follow local rules, which usually mean declining or declaring it and sharing it, and tell your manager
Accept it and say nothing, since the contract is finished and the gift is only a courtesy
Send it back with a sharp note, so that the supplier does not try again with the next contract
Keep it at home, as the contract has ended and there is nothing left for the gift to influence

questions.hint: Transparency and local rules decide.

questions.prompt: Why is a declined gift often recorded?

options.text: So that the person who declined it can claim a reward for good conduct
So that the giver can be asked to collect the gift later if the offer is repeated
So that the department can prove the gift was received if it is questioned
The record shows openness and helps spot patterns of approaches

questions.hint: Records support openness and detect patterns.

questions.prompt: How should hospitality that is lavish and repeated be seen?

options.text: As a perk that comes with seniority and need not be recorded
As a sign of good relationships with suppliers, which helps the work
As a warning sign that may suggest an attempt at influence
As a normal part of the job for senior people, whom suppliers often want to meet

questions.hint: Lavish and repeated hospitality is a risk indicator.

items.title: L7: Speaking up, probation and getting support
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (legislation.gov.uk); Civil Service Management Code
items.body:
The Civil Service Code sets out values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. If you are asked to act in a way you believe is illegal, improper, unethical or in breach of constitutional convention, or you see others doing so, the Code sets out a route. You should first raise the matter with your line manager or someone more senior in your department, or a nominated officer set up for this purpose. If you are not satisfied with the response, you may report the matter to the Civil Service Commission, an independent body. You will not be penalised for raising a concern properly.

The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who make a protected disclosure in the right way, normally to the employer first. It protects against detriment and unfair dismissal, but only if the rules about who you tell and how are followed. This is not a licence to give information to the press, and the Official Secrets Act is not overridden.

Probation is the time for building good habits. You will have regular one-to-ones, objectives, and feedback. Expect to raise issues early, ask for help, and report errors. The usual mistakes in probation are hiding errors, missing deadlines without warning, and treating mandatory learning as optional. A manager who knows about a problem can help; one who finds it late may have to treat it as a performance issue.

Support exists too: employee assistance services, mental health first aiders, networks, trade unions, and adjustments for disability under the Equality Act 2010. Asking for an adjustment is a normal right, not a weakness.

If you disagree with a decision, there are formal routes such as grievance and appeal.

questions.prompt: You are asked to do something you believe is improper. Which is the correct first step under the Code?

options.text: Raise it with your line manager, a senior colleague or the nominated officer
Report it to a newspaper, since publicity is the fastest way of stopping it
Refuse quietly and tell nobody, so as not to cause any trouble in the team
Do it and note your disagreement in your own records, in case it is needed later

questions.hint: The Code sets internal routes first.

questions.prompt: If you are not satisfied with the internal response to your concern, what does the Code allow?

options.text: Sharing it on social media, so that other staff can add their experience
Reporting the matter to the Civil Service Commission, an independent body
Reporting it to your local councillor, who can raise it in public
Taking no further action, since the Code allows only one route for a concern

questions.hint: The Commission is the independent route.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 mainly do?

options.text: It removes the Official Secrets Act for anybody who raises a concern
It gives workers the right to a pay rise after they have made a disclosure
It protects workers who make a protected disclosure in the right way from detriment and unfair dismissal
It allows civil servants to release any information they believe is in the public interest

questions.hint: It protects proper disclosures, normally made to the employer first.

questions.prompt: Why does the 1998 Act not give permission to tell the press?

options.text: Protection depends on following the rules about who is told and how, and the Official Secrets Act is not overridden
It covers disclosures to trade unions only, not to anyone else
It applies only to private firms, so civil servants are not covered by it at all
It lasts for one week after the disclosure is made and then ends

questions.hint: The route matters.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common probation mistake?

options.text: Completing mandatory learning promptly and in good time
Asking questions of colleagues who know the system well
Asking for feedback at one-to-ones and acting upon it
Hiding an error, or missing a deadline without warning

questions.hint: Late discovery causes bigger problems.

questions.prompt: Why does raising a problem early usually help?

options.text: Managers prefer to find out about problems for themselves, whatever the delay
A manager who knows can help, while one who finds out late may have to treat it as a performance issue
Problems vanish by themselves once probation is over, so waiting is harmless
Managers always ignore early reports, so the timing makes no difference

questions.hint: Early reports allow support.

questions.prompt: A new starter needs a workplace adjustment because of a disability. What is the right view?

options.text: Asking for an adjustment suggests that the person is unsuitable for the job
Adjustments are available only after probation has been completed
Adjustments are granted only to senior staff, who have more control over their working week
Asking for an adjustment is a normal right under the Equality Act 2010, not a weakness

questions.hint: The law supports reasonable adjustments.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a form of support commonly offered to staff?

options.text: A free holiday after the first three months in post
A transfer to any role the person asks for
An employee assistance service for confidential advice
A reduction in objectives for the whole of probation

questions.hint: Support services exist for wellbeing.

questions.prompt: You disagree with a probation decision. What routes might exist?

options.text: Grievance and appeal procedures
Telling a journalist who has covered the department
Taking no action, since probation decisions are always final
Posting your view on a professional networking site

questions.hint: Formal routes exist for disagreeing with a decision.

questions.prompt: Under the Code, what should happen to a person who raises a concern properly?

options.text: They should be asked to leave, because the concern shows disloyalty
They should not be penalised for doing so
They should be given a promotion as a reward for doing the right thing
They should be moved to another team while it is looked into

questions.hint: Proper concern-raising is protected.
